## Subject confirmation and scope

- Primary topic: The title “A New Old Play” most reliably refers to the contemporary Chinese feature film directed by Qiu Jiongjiong (邱炯炯), which premiered in 2021 and circulated in major international festivals, including the Locarno Film Festival and the New York Film Festival. Official festival pages and reputable film outlets identify this feature as the notable work associated with the title, making it the primary subject for an encyclopedic article. 
- Alternative uses: If any other notable works share the title, they should be mentioned only if reliable sources confirm their notability and disambiguation is needed. The article should be constrained to the Qiu Jiongjiong film per due weight from reliable sources. 

## Identification and basics to verify (with priority sources)

- Exact title(s): English festival and distributor usage of “A New Old Play”; confirm any alternative English titles if present in regional releases. 
- Original-language title and script, and standard romanization: Official Chinese title (in Chinese characters) and pinyin romanization, as used on sales agent and festival listings; include standard English translation. 
- Year of release: World premiere year (2021) and country/countries of origin. 
- Language(s): Primary language; verify on official pages and press materials. 
- Runtime: Confirm exact runtime (commonly cited around three hours) from festival listings or distributor/sales agent pages. 
- Format and genre: Feature film; genre/format descriptors used by festivals and reputable publications (e.g., historical drama, hybrid theater-cinema). 
- Key production entities:
 - Director: Qiu Jiongjiong (邱炯炯). 
 - Writer(s): Verify on sales agent page and press kit. 
 - Producers and production companies: Confirm via sales agent, press kit, and festival notes. 
 - Cinematographer, editor, art direction, music/sound: Verify credits via official materials and reputable reviews/program notes. 
 - Principal cast with roles: Identify credited performers and role names; note if non-professional actors are used, per interviews and program notes. 

Primary sources to verify these basics:
- Locarno Festival official program page and/or downloadable catalog listing. 
- New York Film Festival (Film at Lincoln Center) official program page. 
- Sales agent and/or distributor official film page and press materials.

- Conception and influences: Director’s stated intentions and artistic background, including relation to Sichuan opera and Chinese theater traditions; gather from interviews and program notes. 
- Cultural context: Historical and cultural setting across mid‑20th‑century China as discussed by critics and official synopses. Attribute analyses to sources. 
- Development timeline: When the project was conceived and developed; funding and production support if documented. 

Recommended sources:
- Director interviews and features in reputable outlets (Film Comment, Variety, Screen Daily, Sight & Sound). 
- Festival program notes (Locarno, NYFF) and Q&As. 
- Sales agent press kit or dossier (credits, synopsis, director’s statement). 

## Plot synopsis

- Concise, neutral summary of the narrative: Outline the premise and structure, sufficient for general readers. Avoid excessive spoilers; align with common practice in established outlets. Attribute interpretive aspects to sources. 
- Commonly cited framing device: Two underworld officials escorting the aging actor to the afterlife, with episodic recollections of a Sichuan opera troupe across political eras; attribute to program notes and critical reviews. 

Recommended sources:
- Festival program synopses (NYFF and Locarno). 
- Reputable reviews (Variety, Screen Daily, Sight & Sound, Film Comment). 

## Themes and style

- Themes: Memory, history, the life of an itinerant theater troupe, the intersection of art and politics, reflections on mid‑20th‑century Chinese society; attribute analyses to critics and scholarly commentary where available. 
- Aesthetics and formal approach: Stage‑like tableaux, theatrical mise‑en‑scène, period set design, long takes, non‑professional performers; describe based on critics and festival notes. 
- Narrative structure: Episodic or chaptered structure; use of allegory and meta‑theatrical techniques; cite critical sources. 

Recommended sources:
- Sight & Sound/BFI, Film Comment features and reviews. 
- Variety and Screen Daily reviews. 
- Festival program notes and Q&As.

## Awards and honors

- Festival prizes: Locarno awards (e.g., Special Jury Prize if applicable); verify via the official festival awards page for the year. 
- Nominations and regional awards: Confirm via official award sites or festival listings; include dates.

- Sight & Sound/BFI and Film Comment essays, year‑end lists.

- Lead section: Concisely identify the film, summarize its notability (festival premiere, key award(s), critical themes and reception), and reflect due weight from reliable sources. Avoid editorializing; attribute significant claims to sources cited in the body.

- Dates and places: Use precise dates and locations verified in sources; include retrieval dates for ratings and databases.

- Confirm the film’s original Chinese title and standardized pinyin. 
- Verify credits: writer, producers, production companies, cinematographer, editor, art direction, music/sound. 
- Verify runtime, languages, and country of origin.

- Collect representative critical analyses from major outlets (minimum 3–5 sources) for themes and style. 

## Notes on source prioritization and reliability

- Prioritize official festival sites, official distributor/sales pages, and major film publications. 
- Avoid user‑generated databases (e.g., IMDb) for factual verification; rely instead on primary (official) and secondary (established media) sources. 
- For Chinese‑language credits or details not covered in English sources, use official Chinese pages (festival/distributor) and provide English translation for key facts.

In a new edition of the series celebrating the work of the greatest auteur directors in history, we delve into our archives to revisit the radical cinema of Chantal Akerman, whose film Jeanne Dielman, 23 quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles, was voted Greatest of All Time in 2022.
